Over the last few weeks, there has been lots of buzz around decision models such as Typesafe AIâs Jev System One model. While classifier models have been around for some time, Jev introduces a new decision model concept into the world of AI â a model that produces bounded structured outputs cheaply, quickly and consistently that can be added into a workflow when a decision is required. These models are capable enough to work over any set of inputs without constantly retraining the model to incorporate new classification categories. This contrasts with the world of Large Language Models (LLMs), which are largely non-deterministic, but are open-ended enough to reason and generate text and tool calls for agentic workloads.Â

Today, weâre releasing two Cloudflare-trained decision models, Clef and Clef-flash, hosted on Workers AI . Clef is currently the leader when evaluated against the Jev Decision Index , you can view full results on the live benchmark demo site . These models are smarter, faster, and fully Jev-API compatible, so you can experiment with these hosted models easily. Weâre fully open-sourcing these models on Hugging Face under an Apache 2.0 license for you to run locally and experiment with yourselves.Â

Lastly, weâre excited to debut our new reinforcement learning (RL) product, which allows customers to fine-tune Clef to suit their use cases as well.

## What is a decision model?

A decision model makes classifications to help agents decide how to act, based on certain probabilities. For example, you can pass in a customer support message (inputs) and ask if it is urgent and which team should handle it. A decision model will return typed answers with probabilities (outputs), which your code can use to route the ticket, trigger an escalation, or defer to a human. This means that a human does not necessarily need to be in the loop for agentic decisions anymore â agents can programmatically gather context, make decisions, and take actions on tasks, or defer to a human when needed.

Specifically at Cloudflare, weâve been testing our new Clef model on our Threat Intelligence team to help us classify website domains. By giving a domain to Clef (with Browser Run) it can quickly identify categories that the domain falls under â for example, it might classify a domain with a 95% chance it is a fashion website, 85% ecommerce, <1% phishing, etc. This classification took our Clef model 2.2s to fetch, render, and classify the website. In contrast, our fastest general LLM gpt-oss-120b took 4.7s in the same workflow, and only returned two classifications. As a user, you can imagine how a 2x savings in latency and results can help us improve our threat intelligence workflows and be faster in identifying malicious or legitimate domains. Generalize this to any use case where you need to make quick programmatic decisions, and you unlock powerful agentic workflows that are able to autonomously decide, reason, and execute.

In music theory, a clef is a symbol placed at the beginning of a musical staff that assigns specific pitch names to the lines and spaces. A decision model is analogous to a music clef because it helps define the domain of the context and the subsequent notes (actions) that follow it. We chose Clef as the name of our family of decision models, as it serves similar purposes, and the CF hearkens to Cloudflare.

## How is Clef different from other decision models?

Although the market is getting increasingly saturated with decision models, Clef has some unique properties that make us excited to release it to the public. First, it has a vision encoder so itâs able to take in images and classify visual content. This is different from Jev, which only does text classification today. Secondly, our model has a 64k context window (compared to Jevâs 32k), which allows users to squeeze more input state for the model to classify against.

Third, our model is accurate and powerful, scoring competitively against other decision models on the market across various quality benchmarks. ### How we trained Clef

In the same week that Jev came out, we posted about some experiments we had with our own homegrown decision model. Our demo goes into how we adapted the DiffusionGemma model to output deterministic probabilities by exposing the logprobs that are generated by a large language model. Our initial approach built upon independent research by Matt Mastracci , who has been active in the machine learning (ML) community with sharing new ideas and pull requests to vLLM inference engine to make DiffusionGemma support stronger.

Clef builds upon this concept, but uses a different base model as the backbone. We currently use Qwen as the base model and post-trained it to suit decision model use cases. During inference, Clef uses Qwen for a prefill-only pass, then scores the valid schema choices in parallel. The decision step is non-autoregressive, so thereâs no intermediate text to generate token by token, making Clef significantly faster than autoregressive LLMs. Rather than generating intermediate text to produce structured answers, Clef and Clef-flash derive schema choices directly from internal backbone representations. This approach relies on a specialized two-stage attention routing process: every valid choice extracts context relevant to the prompt, allowing individual field parameters to cross-attend with other fields and back to the original payload prior to scoring. By leveraging a lexical prior, the model preserves semantic intent across options. Ultimately, the architecture unites option-specific evidence routing, joint cross-field attention, and schema-bound scoring.

By freezing Qwen3.8-27B for Clef and Qwen3.5-9B for Clef-flash, we jointly optimized the routing head alongside rank-256 low-rank adapters. Our post-training utilizes label-smoothed cross-entropy for valid schema outputs paired with a Brier loss to refine probability calibration. This training leverages our own internal synthetic datasets permutating field orders, prompts, and schema structures. We also developed Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions (RLCD) to serve as a secondary optimization target, granting partial credit to adjacent ordinal choices, rewarding fully precise record outputs, and applying a reference penalty to prevent distribution shift, giving us better accuracy and generalization.

This means that we were able to achieve a few novel things with Clef: we improved accuracy of the model in classification, constrained it to output only probabilities instead of text generation, and made it faster than Jev and the base Qwen models.

### How fine-tuning can extend the capabilities of Clef

We heard a lot of internal use cases that required fine-tuning our Clef model to be built into our agentic workflows at Cloudflare. For example, internal teams want a classifier model to be able to evaluate Trust & Safety submissions, help us triage Cloudflare Support requests, or even to be built-in to our Bot products to decide if a crawler is a good bot or bad bot.

These use cases are incredibly specific and we have had many years of labelled decisions that we could use to train a specific classifier. When you fine-tune a model, you may give up some general purpose performance in exchange for higher accuracy in a specific domain.. Because Cloudflare has more than 15 years of network data across different domains, we can fine-tune a model to fit these specific use cases which is more accurate and faster than our generic Clef model. Weâre working with internal teams already to figure out how we can post-train Clef to create powerful ML models that boost our impact and improve workflows across Cloudflare. These internal teams and use cases are the next remit of our new FDE fine-tuning team and basis for our reinforcement learning (RL) product.

Optimizing your site for AI is of little use if AI can't find it. The answer to someone's question may already be on your website: the installation guide you spent a week writing, or a first-hand account of using a product, with the details that make the difference for whether they buy it. As more people turn to AI for help, you want those systems to find your work, represent it accurately, and send interested people your way. You also want control over how they access your site.

Cloudflare and OpenAI launched a research pilot Â in July 2026 with those interests in mind. We wanted to find out whether signals from Cloudflareâs network could help ChatGPT users discover new content more efficiently.

Today, weâre sharing early results. So far, the answer is a resounding yes: the pilot has brought previously unknown pages into OpenAIâs search index, giving ChatGPT more sources to draw on to help people find relevant, timely information. Along the way, weâve learned more about what makes a page worth discovering and how AI systems use the web.

## Finding more of the web

The web is full of specifics. Someone fixing a washing machine needs the manual for their exact model. Someone applying for a passport needs the current requirements and fees. Someone choosing a local restaurant needs its latest menu and opening hours. Finding the right page can be the difference between a wrong answer and one that actually helps. These pages can be valuable even if few other sites link to them.

In the previous version of the web, discoverability was getting to the top of a search result page. It was then up to the human who visited your page to determine the value of the information, book that table, apply for that passport. As people increasingly rely on AI to find information and complete tasks, discoverability matters in new ways. AI systems need to find the right sources, understand what's useful, and connect people with relevant information â whether that's through an answer, a citation, or a visit to the website itself.

Cloudflare's network provides signals that can help OpenAIâs search crawler discover more useful pages across the web to surface to ChatGPT users. OpenAI then independently evaluates and ranks how those pages appear based on how relevant and helpful they are. Together, this creates a feedback loop that can improve both discovery and the quality of information people find.

This joint pilot, which used a participating cohort of ~1% of Cloudflareâs total network, has enabled OpenAI to discover and index hundreds of millions of new web pages, helping people discover more useful content and get more questions answered through ChatGPT. By linking back to relevant sources, ChatGPT Search also gives people a way to explore the original content and discover the websites and publishers behind it.

With GPT-6 and Intelligent UI , OpenAI is also making ChatGPT an even better place to shop, learn, and find answers, with more visual, interactive experiences tailored to what people need. This work complements these advances by helping ChatGPT discover more useful, up-to-date information from across the web.

## From discovery to useful answers

Finding a URL is only the start. We need to know whether it leads to a page someone can access, whether that page offers anything distinct, and what it might help someone do.

Weâve learned, for example, how easily automated traffic can make a nonexistent page look interesting. Bots repeatedly ask for files that arenât there. Some sites redirect almost any address to their homepage. Other addresses lead to copies of the same content. Recognizing these patterns gives us a way to cut wasted work before a crawler fetches the page, and improve efficiency in a way that benefits site owners.

We're also testing signals that identify and flag potentially harmful pages, adding another layer of information to support safer, more reliable discovery. A legitimate site can have a single compromised page, such as a fake login form planted by an attacker. Flagging that one page, rather than the whole domain, keeps people safe without penalizing the site owner. Early results suggest these signals can help identify pages that should be kept out of an index.

## Making discovery easier

As more people use AI to discover information, website owners have new opportunities to reach interested audiences. For those who choose to make their content available to AI systems, these improvements make discovery easier and more efficient.

Keeping up by fetching every page more often would be expensive for everyone. For a website owner, a crawler that repeatedly downloads an unchanged page adds load without bringing any benefit.

The signals above are how we avoid that. Filtering keeps crawlers away from pages that don't exist or that redirect elsewhere. Change signals tell them when a page is worth another visit, and when it isn't.

There's a balance to get right. Finding new pages can initially increase crawling as those pages are evaluated and indexed. The goal is to keep discovering and stay current while reducing the work that takes. For Cloudflare customers, that means less unnecessary load. For OpenAI, it means more of its search resources are spent on information that helps people.

## Making it worthwhile to participate

The next phase will build on what weâve learned: improve the selection of pages, test faster and more reliable change signals, and measure what happens after content is discovered.

Weâre continuing to work with OpenAI to understand how better site discovery can translate into real business outcomes, and weâll keep sharing what we learn along the way.

Domain ownersâ choices matter throughout. A signal about a page doesnât grant permission to access it. This research uses metadata about the web for search and discovery, rather than sharing page content for model training.
